data.title: Most pri Bratislave – the first Old Slavic sanctuary in Slovakia
data.excerpt: Little is known about how the Slavs living between the Danube and the Tatras accepted Christianity, and until recently not a single Old Slavic sanctuary was known from Slovak territory. That changed in the 1980s, when a rescue excavation at a gravel pit at Most pri Bratislave uncovered a quarter-circle trench more than 27 m long, a hearth fuelled with oak and the skull of an ox – a cult place dedicated to the thunder god Perún.
data.metaTitle: Most pri Bratislave – first Old Slavic sanctuary
data.metaDescription: A pagan cult place at Most pri Bratislave, regarded by Vladimír Turčan as the first Old Slavic sanctuary known from Slovak territory.

children.text: Light on the riddle of a Slavic cult place

We know very little about how our Slavic ancestors accepted Christianity. The first written report that brings at least a little light into the Christianisation of this country concerns the consecration of a church on the estate of Prince Pribina in Nitra by Archbishop Adalram of Salzburg in 828. Historians rightly point out, however, that this was most probably a formal act of a political nature. In those years the new faith between the Danube and the Tatras was still far from victorious.

What is more, it seems that not even members of the Slavic elite had themselves baptised. Pribina himself remained faithful to the faith of his ancestors and accepted baptism only in 837 at Traismauer in Austria. True, that was already after his expulsion from Nitra, when his protectors gave him no other choice.

At the time of the consecration of the church in Nitra, then, the Slavs professed the faith of their ancestors. It was a polytheistic religion, that is, unlike monotheism they believed in the existence of several gods. At the head of the Old Slavic pantheon stood Perún, ruler of lightning and fire. Another important god was Svarog, associated with fire, heavenly light and warmth, as was his son Svarožič. The original gods in whom the Slavs believed while still in their ancestral homeland also included Stribog, god of the sky and the wind, Chors, perhaps connected with the moon, Simargl, whose competences are now unclear to us, and the only representative of the fair sex, Mokoš, who protected the harvest. The pantheon of the Old Slavic gods has thus been reconstructed relatively well from various written records. Until the acceptance of Christianity, our ancestors too bowed down to these deities.

Until recently, however, we asked in vain where this took place. From Slovak territory we knew no Old Slavic sanctuary at all. As late as 1960 the outstanding Czech archaeologist and Slavist Rudolf Turek could write in his survey Pravěk Československa (The Prehistory of Czechoslovakia) that „pohanský kult našich předků neznal chrámů“ – ‘the pagan cult of our ancestors knew no temples’. That the neighbouring Slavic tribes did build sanctuaries was known, for example, from archaeological finds in the milieu of the East Slavs, from Poland and from present-day Germany. Only the excavations of Moravian and Czech archaeologists at Mikulčice, Staré Město near Uherské Hradiště, Pohansko near Břeclav and Hradsko in the Kokořín area brought evidence that the Slavs of central Europe too worshipped their gods in sanctuaries. These, however, differed architecturally from one another, and to define a uniform ground plan, as well as to reconstruct the course of the rites in such a cult feature, is very difficult. The answer to the question of what the cult places of our Slavic ancestors looked like could therefore be brought only by a discovery made by archaeologists.
An interesting find

During one of the rescue excavations it finally came about unexpectedly. On the edge of the village of Most pri Bratislave, on the easternmost tip of Žitný ostrov, there was in the 1980s a large and deep pit left after the extraction of gravel. Its bottom was gradually being filled with rubbish. And above it, in the wall of the pit, dark patches stood out – the fills of ancient sunken features. At that time Etela Studeníková, then a member of staff of the Archaeological Museum of the Slovak National Museum (SNM), travelled through the village every day to the excavation of Hallstatt-period burial mounds at Dolné Janíky, today known to foreign scholars as well. The features did not escape her attention. The archaeological excavation established that these were traces of a hitherto unknown Slavic settlement. The rescue excavation of the site, which was threatened by the spontaneous collapse of the gravel walls, lasted three years. Fourteen features were investigated. They were standard pits of amorphous shape with basin-like sloping sides, to which archaeologists attribute the function of agricultural or technical features. All except one…

The surprise, however, was brought by precisely that one. It lay roughly in the central part of the investigated area. In shape it resembled a segment of a circle, formed by a trench more than 27 m long and at most 280 cm wide. The width of the feature varied, however, narrowing towards the ends of the segment. The semicircle, or rather quarter-circle, opened towards the east. The feature, with its middle part widened on both sides, was sunk 20–50 cm into the subsoil. Irregularly spaced post holes were found around its circumference. Four post holes in the northern part formed a rectangle in which lay a hearth filled with ash and charcoal. The horn of an ox was found beside the hearth. North of the hearth there were burnt amorphous areas and several local thin grey layers, probably the remains of small, short-lived hearths. Sherds and animal bones were found in the fill of the feature.

children.text: That is all that remains of the very first known Old Slavic sanctuary in Slovakia. The sherds found showed that the cult feature dates from the second half of the 8th century to the beginning of the following century. Interestingly, the most convincing argument for this dating was not the Slavic sherds, although these clearly predominated in the fill of the feature, but several fragments of nomadic bell-shaped clay lids. The problem is that Slavic pot-shaped vessels with an S-shaped profile, decorated on the upper part of the body with incised wavy lines or horizontal grooving, were made over a relatively long time, during which above all the production technology changed (that is, the composition of the potting clay, the way the vessel was shaped, the profile of the mouth, the construction of the pottery kilns). At the central hillforts the potters produced better-quality ware in the same period than the craftsmen in village settlements. Precise dating of a find spot on the basis of sherds is therefore not always unambiguous. The nomadic “bells”, which served for cooking, were in use for a much shorter time.

children.text: More complicated than dating the sanctuary was the more precise determination of the function of this unusual find and its reconstruction. The ground plan itself served as the starting point. A trench dug in the form of a circular segment is already known from several Old Slavic sanctuaries in Moravia and Bohemia, for example at Uherské Hradiště-Sady or at Mikulčice. Archaeologists also attribute cult significance to the positively mammoth feature at Stará Kouřim. This find, extraordinary in both its dimensions and its importance, was a slightly curving ditch 4 m deep and up to 130 m long, separating a small cemetery beside a little lake from the occupied area of an early medieval hillfort. Its complex layout in itself calls for exceptional attention – it proves that among the Slavs the world of the dead had to be separated from the world of the living. From other sources we know that, in the conception of the Slavs, earthly and otherworldly existence were separated precisely by water. The similarity to Charon and the ferrying of the dead in a boat is certainly no coincidence in this case.

children.text: A place made for the worship of the gods

Let us try to apply this finding to the sanctuary at Most pri Bratislave. In the 8th century Žitný ostrov was an infertile country full of marshes and of blind and side arms of the Danube, which kept changing after the spring and autumn floods. No wonder that archaeologists know no permanent settlement from this region, at least as far as the Early Middle Ages are concerned. The isolated traces of the presence of Slavs that are found point rather to the temporary stay of fishermen, hunters and the like. Yet it was precisely with such a natural environment that the Old Slavs associated their notions of a mysterious place in which it was possible to address the gods. It was a site separated from the surrounding world by waters, marshes and little lakes. Nor, it seems, did they choose at random the particular spot where they built the sanctuary. The original vegetation cover, however, was long ago destroyed by human activity, and the river network has changed as well.

In attempting to reconstruct the above-ground parts of the sanctuary one can rely on several details established during the archaeological excavation. The post holes that lined the outer and inner side of the edge, insignificant at first sight, also tell us something about the original appearance of the Old Slavic cult place. According to the account of the Russian chronicler Nestor, the Slavs used to place urns with the cremated remains of the dead on posts. In the case of our sanctuary, however, such an interpretation is out of the question, because in the 8th century the Slavs of central Europe already laid the uncremated remains of the deceased in graves (the corresponding archaeological term is inhumation graves). A solution is offered by the fact that the post holes occur in pairs. This fact strikingly recalls a find from the Slavic settlement at the site of Fischerinsel near Neubrandenburg in Germany. A wooden figurine of a Slavic deity with two heads and two joined bodies was found there, a kind of double deity.

children.text: Greater certainty in interpretation is offered by the group of four post holes in the southern part of the sanctuary. Their arrangement and their mutual distance reveal that a lighter wooden canopy undoubtedly stood here. Similar traces were identified at Uherské Hradiště-Sady. Given the position of the cult feature within the area of a cemetery, it could have served as a place for laying out the remains of a human body “on a bier”. Such an interpretation is, however, not logically possible for Most pri Bratislave, since there were no graves in the feature.

blocks.caption: Kupala – a celebration of the summer solstice.

children.text: The answer to the question of the function of the canopy is offered by the discovery of a hearth inside it. It is a large hearth strongly fired to a red colour. Only a strong fire burning over a long period leaves such a trace. The canopy thus served to protect the “eternal fire” from the rain. Surely not by chance, this in turn reminds us of the fire maintained in ancient Rome by the Vestals – if it went out, a Vestal faced death. Scholars link the maintenance of fires among the Slavs with the cult of the god Perún. Among the East Slavs oak was used as cult fuel. It is therefore no surprise that from the charcoal of the hearth mentioned the palynologist Eduard Krippel determined that it was Quercus, that is oak – the sacred tree of the Slavs, dedicated to the thunder god Perún. The Baltic Slavs even venerated whole oak woods, and from the Balkans religious rites beneath oaks are documented as late as the Middle Ages.

children.text: Another detail also deserves attention. An animal skull was found right beside the post holes on the western edge of the trench. It was so badly destroyed that only with great effort did the archaeozoologist Alena Šefčáková succeed, at the Natural History Museum of the SNM, in determining that it was an ox. Nor is this animal unknown in Slavic mythology – it was dedicated to Perún. Bulls’ horns decorated the hall sanctuaries of the Baltic Slavs, and the skull probably fulfilled a similar function in our sanctuary too. It was probably placed in the middle of the front wall of the wooden canopy mentioned.

While the southern part of the sanctuary was by all appearances the official space, that is, the place where cult rites connected with the whole clan or tribe took place in the presence of a pagan priest (a cult personage) and probably only at the time of the annual feasts, the northern part was probably reserved for private rites. This can be inferred from the fact that in this half no larger hearth or traces of a structure were found, but only a larger number of smaller hearths which, judging by the colouring of the soil, were short-lived. Here individual families or individuals probably made offerings to Perún.

blocks.alt: A visualisation of the Old Slavic sanctuary (author: Haden Sutton)

children.text: Who prayed in the sanctuary at Most?

Where the tribes lived whose members came to bow down at today’s Most pri Bratislave can be deduced from the sherds mentioned, found in the fill of the trench. Besides south-western Slovakia, where we find similar pottery at settlements of the 8th to the beginning of the 9th century, the inhabitants of settlements lying south of the Danube also came here. In view of the fragments of nomadic bell-shaped lids, they need not have been only Slavs. On the other hand, in certain regions this inventory could also have been used by members of other ethnic groups. The ground plan of the cult feature at Most pri Bratislave suggests that the rites took place here under the open sky. That was typical of the Slavs of central Europe, because the Baltic Slavs, for example, built hall sanctuaries to which, according to the records of the German priest Helmold, only the pagan priest had access. At Most pri Bratislave the space beneath the covering canopy was probably intended for him. Perhaps it was he who was responsible for ensuring that the flames of the “eternal fire” never went out. With that, however, we are moving from the analysis and reconstruction of an archaeological find of an Old Slavic cult place to considerations that go beyond the scope of archaeological and historical possibilities.

Since objects from the middle of the 9th century are missing among the finds from Most pri Bratislave, the sanctuary apparently came to an end in this period. Either this happened after a change in tribal relations and the faithful went to bow down to Perún at another mysterious place, or the cult place came to an end with the arrival of Christianity. The absence of later finds from the whole region suggests that the Slavs never returned to the place where the Old Slavic sanctuary stood, and the cult place was covered over by the floodplain forests of Žitný ostrov.
PhDr. Vladimír Turčan (1952),

works at the Archaeological Museum of the SNM in Bratislava. He specialises in the archaeology of the Roman and the Slavic period. He has taken part in archaeological excavations of the Roman-period fort at Stupava and of several Slavic and Germanic settlements.
